Why do ranchers not sell their ranches, then?
February 17, 1969

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext: Because they like ranching, and because they are more optimistic than are hon. members of the N.D.P. They believe better days are ahead.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext: The last few weeks have done nothing to foster that optimism.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
I should like to show why a ranch valued at $100,000 ostensibly should return only $1,200, $1,500 or $2,280 as profit on invested capital. The answer lies in the fact that the figures respecting value are entirely illusory. The ranches in question are not worth $100,000. What has happened is that some fortunate rancher has recently sold his ranch at a totally inflated price, and other ranchers near him are listed as being equally valuable. That value figure has no basis in reality. It is a figure on a piece of paper. The man who collects estate taxes refers to the figure on that piece of paper in his calculations, to the misfortunate of many ranchers. That is why I was particularly interested in the comments of the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar. He spoke of farms that were approximately as valuable as the ranches I have mentioned. From his remarks, I judge that farmers in his area find themselves in the same sort of situation as ranchers in my area.
I now wish to speak about the new estate tax being applied to a $100,000 estate. I wish to take the case in which the tax bears most heavily, the case where the estate is left outright by a widower to one son, and not to two or three. Under the present law that son will pay $10,200 in estate tax. Under the proposed law he would pay $13,200, an increase of $3,000, which is considerable and which threatens the existence of the family farm.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
However, if this $3,000 increase is paid out over five years, that will mean that $600 a year extra per year will be paid. This is considerably less than some of the gloom and doom people have suggested would have to be paid. I doubt that many hundred thousand dollar ranches will go under for the sake of a six hundred dollar per year payment. A point was raised by a member of the Ralliement Creditiste. It is a different philosophic question but one, with which I think we should deal. The province of Alberta has already taken a stand on this

matter. The question is, does the state have a proper right to collect estate taxes?
Estates are capital. They are savings and profit put aside by men who during their lifetime paid a tax on their incomes. Is it right for the state to take a second bite of the fruit of that man's labour when he dies? The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Dumont) summed up the position of his party at page 5192 of Hansard. I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to point out to the Minister of Finance that we, of the Ralliement Creditiste, are opposed to any tax at all in Canada, and that the very fact of levying a tax on private estates discourages private enterprise. That is why we say that the Minister of Finance should seek another formula.
It seems the state not only has the right to impose estate taxes, but in my opinion it has a duty. The alternative is very clear. Unless estate taxes are used to prevent the pyramiding of family wealth, then it must follow we are going to move increasingly into a hereditary aristocracy of wealth in this country. It will not be basically from a titled aristocracy. It will gain power in the nation's political affairs by virtue of birth rather than by virtue of individual worth. I am convinced that this or any other form of class system is bad for Canada.
Canada has not suffered from the lack of a Rockefeller or Dupont family, and I am very sure we have not suffered from the lack of the Krupp family of Germany. I ask those members of the Ralliement Creditiste who oppose this bill on the basic principle that estate taxes are wrong if they are prepared to add to the power which already exists in an aristocracy of wealth in this nation. If so, why not go the next logical step and have hereditary lords in this country? Perhaps they would prefer to have the Senate seats hereditary. I cannot be convinced this would be good for Canada.
In closing, Mr. Speaker I would say this is generally good legislation for Canada. The original weak points have been largely eliminated. It has been vastly improved and is more just than the present estate tax legislation. For these reasons, I have no hesitation in supporting it.

There have been certain discussions, Mr. Speaker, about the government reorganization bill which was introduced on first reading today. I think there is general agreement it would be preferable to deal with the bill in committee of the whole, rather than refer it to any standing committee. It has been suggested, pursuant to standing order 74 (2), that it would be necessary to make a special order of the house in this regard. Without prejudice to any views or debate which may take place on the interpretation of that order, I would like to propose the following order to deal with the reorganization bill:
That an order be made, that upon second reading of the bill entitled "An act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters relating or incidental thereto" the said bill stand referred to the committee of the whole house.

That remains to be seen. When the minister first announced these changes back on October 22, 1968, he so swaddled them in candy floss that many of us were misled into believing that they were really great tax concessions, an improvement, a reform. We admit this. At that time, the minister assured us he was not bringing in these changes simply to raise more revenue. He just wanted to make some modest changes that would correct injustices but still yield about the same amount of revenue for the federal treasury.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
On October 22 the minister said, as reported at page 1685 of Hansard:
I propose that the loss of revenue arising from this long awaited reform of the exemption structure be made up by raising the rates on the rest of the estate-
It is difficult to predict accurately the revenue effects of changes in estate taxes but I have aimed at maintaining the same total over-all revenue-
In other words, the minister did not intend this measure as a revenue-producing measure but rather as a measure to correct inequity and injustice which he believed existed in the old act. I said "he believed" but I am not quite sure what he believed. If my figures are correct, the minister could not possibly have brought forward these proposals as an economic measure. The revenue to which he referred amounts to a mere pittance by today's standards of federal budgeting. In comparison with total federal revenue, the proportion of that revenue raised by estate and gift taxation is equally small.
In his budget speech the minister forecast total budgetary revenues amounting to between $10 billion and $11 billion, and revenue from estate taxes amounting to $110 million. According to my calculation, the estate taxes provide just a shade over one per cent of total revenue, a rate borne out over the
February 17, 1969

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act past five years according to budget paper figures. But that is not the end of the story. We must remember that 75 per cent of the revenue collected federally by estate taxation goes to the provinces. So, the figure the minister is actually concerned with, as the federal minister charged with running the federal government shop, is only somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30 million. An amount of $30 million, in a budget with a total revenues of more than $10 billion, is not an item which should cause the minister the concern, work and argument already involved in trying to foist this tax upon the Canadian taxpayer.
It is interesting that, in respect of the provinces, in his speech the minister said:
We recognize the special interest of the provinces in this field of taxation but believe that parliament should keep a share in it for its indirect benefits in the enforcing of the Income Tax Act as well as its direct benefits in revenue.
Recognizing the particular interest of the provinces in this field, it is strange the minister did not consult them before making such a drastic change; or perhaps he did and did not like what he heard from them. According to the Toronto Telegram of December 18, Saskatchewan's Premier Thatcher said:
We made the strongest possible representations to Ottawa not to proceed with these changes.
Mr. Thatcher then went on to say that his government would bring in legislation to rebate to the people concerned the 75 per cent of estate tax revenue received from Ottawa. This has already been done in the province of Alberta. There is a strong probability that it will be done in the province of Manitoba. Other provinces, in recent years, have shown every indication of getting out of this unpalatable field of taxation. But the minister and his colleagues in the cabinet cling ghoulishly to death duties as a source of revenue, or so they say. So, we come back once again to the big question mark; why the radical changes in the estate and gift tax setup? This is what the people are asking.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member who interrupted, may I say that perhaps he does not have any manners but he certainly has no political sense. Many of us know that he sat for years as an Independent member because no party would have him. I am surprised that the Liberals have taken him now.
In the same speech, the minister said that the forced sale of a farm or family business had seldom occurred in connection with payment of estate taxes. This may well be true, but this was in the past. It was before the Benson thumbscrew was applied, as I believe it is being applied now. Again, at the same meeting the minister said:
I should remind you that the vast majority of Canadians have not, and will not now, pay any estate tax.
This certainly may be true, now that they have raised the exemption to $50,000, for certain classes of people only. This is class, or discriminatory, legislation and cannot do justice to all Canadians. It is directed toward the urban centres and is introduced for a political purpose. What the minister neglected to explain was that his new regulations dropped the floor for taxable estates down to $20,000.
February 17, 1969

This is still the floor. Who is he trying to kid by saying that the vast majority of Canadians will not now be taxable? The minister has steadfastly refused to explain the real purpose of this tax. On the basis of his own statements and his own figures it cannot be an economic measure. I presume even this government would not be fatuous enough to bring in a piece of legislation without any purpose whatever. If, then, we presume the proposals to have a purpose-and we have seen that this purpose cannot be justified in economic terms-we are driven to the conclusion that this measure is not indeed an economic measure but a social measure. We ask why. Maybe the New Democratic party members should ask why. It is my belief that it is a social measure and a social measure of a revolutionary kind.
I believe that if this parliament adopts these tax and gift tax resolutions, Canada will see the disappearance within a short time of that great segment of her people who still seek to live by individual initiative and individual enterprise. I am not alone in this belief. A host of newspaper editorial writers, commentators and tax experts have made the same prediction. Premier Thatcher said this "outrageous" measure meant the "end of the family farm". We in western Canada believe that. The members of the N.D.P. party in western Canada believe that. They pleaded with the minister not to impose this tax.
Mr. William Purdy, president of the Canadian Construction Association, was reported in the Ottawa Journal of January 22 as saying that the estate tax as proposed "will make it virtually impossible for family-owned construction firms to be passed on to the next generation". He pointed out that of 17,000 construction companies in Canada fewer than 200 were public companies, and that family firms did more than 90 per cent of the annual construction business in Canada. In an article generally favourable to the minister and the minister's works, Pat Carney wrote in the Ottawa Journal of January 21:
-the children will pay for mom's exemption-
At another point this article reads:
-the bugs in the new system centre around the fact that the happy family unit envisaged by Benson may not reflect the facts of life.

The Saint John Telegraph-Journal of December 4 points out editorially:
With today's less valuable dollar, the reduction- down to a floor of $20,000-will extend the tax to almost anyone who has a small home and a modest insurance program, or a store or a business, or virtually any farm capable of providing even a simple living.
As hon. members know, December 4 was before the minister brought in this $50,000 gimmick to pacify his backbenchers. This was the purpose of it. I am sure the minister does not believe this is fair taxation. The social implications of this measure, the necessity of gathering even the smallest of independent Canadian fish in the net, explains the otherwise inexplicable matter of lowering the level at which an estate becomes taxable. I do not know how the minister decided on this tax. In western Canada, as a Liberal member said a few moments ago, we have seen farmers leave farms valued at $100,000. Some of those estates valued at more than $100,000 may have been left because of climatic conditions or other circumstances; so how can you assess an estate at $100,000, when it has no liquid assets? There has to be some other formula arrived at.
This type of social regimentation is in the Liberal tradition. This is the type of socialistic state planning of my hon. friends in the N.D.P., which the former prime minister

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act bought by the package from one of his advisers; I think it was Tom Kent. This is the type of Liberal, bureaucratic control about which we heard something a short time ago when we were dealing with the agricultural bill. It is the type of Liberal, bureaucratic control sought by the erstwhile minister of national health and welfare when he brought in social security cards and social security numbers. This was done for a purpose; it is all part of the over-all picture.
To the Liberal ministerial mind, to the minds of the mandarins of the civil service, to the minds of the army of soulless Ottawa bureaucrats, no Canadian must be allowed to stand in the way of state planning, state guidance and state administration. The aim is to render every Canadian capable of being controlled by a central computer. This is why we have numbers. Therefore, the ordinary Canadian must be registered, concentrated, made subject to control and allowed no leeway for individual enterprise or individual initiative. That is the aim of this measure; and it is an aim that will be achieved in a frighteningly few years if this type of measure passes the house.
The same sort of group of small, independently minded citizens stood in the way of the Soviet state machine in the early thirties. Hon. members opposite laughed a few moments ago when I mentioned the Soviet regime of the early thirties. Stalin's solution was collectivism, transportation or murder. We are softer and more subtle. But the end result will be the same, the death of a class. I referred to this earlier.
The hallmark of Liberal legislation has always been its absence of humanity. Liberal ministers and senior civil servants have over the years become almost indistinguishable. They have never considered Canadian citizens as human as human beings but only as economic and social units. To realize this, one has only to recall the recommendations made some years ago by the high priest of Liberal theorists, Walter Gordon, when he sought to solve the problems of Cape Breton. His solution was simple, move the people to Upper Canada.
The same sort of philosophy is apparent today. One has but to examine the government's attitude to farmers both east and west to realize the callous disregard they have for people and their obsession with the abstract and the theoretical. One excellent example of this is their present approach to the hard-hit east coast fishing industry. We heard about


this problem just a few days ago. What was the government's answer to the plea to save this basic Canadian industry? The Liberals' answer was: Let it die. My colleagues from Newfoundland will verify this fact. The answer of the government was: Let it go by default, and put the people on some form of government subsistence. This is the Liberals' answer to these problems.
The Liberals say: Don't bother about things like human dignity or a man's desire to fend for himself and his family. It is much easier from a social planner's point of view to have everyone's name on a list, numbered and carded for a computer. It is more efficient to issue a series of identical cheques at regular intervals than to find ways of assisting people to look after themselves and to compete with their fellows on an equal footing.
The same sort of soulless, technological approach lies behind the minister's estate tax proposals. Family economic units are a nuisance. Scattered groups of independently-minded Canadians are a nuisance. They foul up the bureaucrats and are not adaptable to smooth, business-machine processing. The attitude of the Liberal party is: Get rid of them, wipe them out, regiment them along with their brothers in the huge, industrialized, urban centres.
I realize that these measures will hit the various pockets of individual enterprise left in urban centres just as hard as they will hit Canada's agricultural community, but at the moment my chief concern is with the impact they will have on rural Canada. To my mind, these tax proposals which set out new tax minimums and higher accelerated rates of taxation must be assessed as part of the whole system of applying federal estate taxes. They are bad enough of themselves, but when applied on valuation figures arbitrarily set by the taxing authority, with an accompanying demand for quick payment they could prove disastrous.
We all know something of the punitive and unrealistic figures arrived a by federal government evaluators. Not only do they seldom take cognizance of local market conditions and local valuation practice, but they take no recognition whatsoever of the low points in regional economic cycles such as we had two years ago in western Canada and again last year. In western Canada, the past season and the general condition of the world market for agricultural produce almost guarantee that anyone selling a farm there today will have to do so at a ruinous price, a
February 17, 1969

sacrifice-if indeed it can be sold at all. Judging by past practice, the federal estate tax valuation figures will take no notice of these conditions and that could mean the extinction of many rural enterprises.
I, for one, do not accept at face value the minister's bland assurances that no Canadian heir will suffer under these new proposals. If they are to be as he has said, if they are to be applied as he has said, then common sense indicates that many, many new taxpayers will be gathered into his tax net and many, many Canadians will be subject to an unjust and confiscatory tax bite.
Many of the criticisms that can be made about this legislation have been made, and well made, by previous speakers. Heaven alone knows, there is enough room for an army of critics here. However, I do not want to labour my opposition to this measure much longer. There is only one further point I wish to make. It concerns the warning given in the introduction of the new tax proposals of very ominous things to come. I believe it is fair to say that the minister's proposals are simply feelers for more sweeping tax "reforms" to come; a trial balloon, a toe in the water. If this be so, it is my conviction that the minister's manner of introducing so-called reforms is entirely unsuitable, and that he is the last person to handle such a monumental task.

maintopic: PRINCIPLE OF ACCESSIBILITY OF REPORTS AND STUDIES UNDERTAKEN FOR THE GOVERNMENT BY OUTSIDE PROFESSIONAL GROUPS
PRINCIPLE OF ACCESSIBILITY OF REPORTS AND STUDIES UNDERTAKEN FOR THE GOVERNMENT BY OUTSIDE PROFESSIONAL GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principle that I wish to discuss on the adjournment debate has to do with the availability of government information. The particular issue is that in these days when government is becoming more and more sophisticated and many studies from outside sources will have to be called for it is important to parliament that the results of
DEBATES	5631
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion these studies be made available to us. One of the examples that comes to mind is the rather famous case of the Winnipeg overhaul base. As the member for Fundy-Royal, I have not a clue as to whether the overhaul base should be in Winnipeg or Montreal, and it does not really matter to me in which spot it is. In trying to assess the proper location for this site, the government called for an independent study by management consultants which produced what is known as the Thompson report. The difficulty is that the results of this report were never made available to the very people who were expected to pass judgment on the government's decision to phase out the base. Just as such a situation took place in Winnipeg, so too did it take place in almost every area. In fact what led me to this question is the fact that a great deal more reliance is going to be placed by the government on outside experts to give the government the benefit of their information. I, myself, prefer the system in Sweden which has worked very well for some decades where all information, unless it has to do with the fundamental issue of the safety and security of the state, is a matter of public record. I think it is known by text writers on the subject as the goldfish bowl principle, which is a rather descriptive term to use. In Sweden any information from reports or studies is automatically published, unless the safety of the state is involved.
I want to have the assurance of the administration that, if they cannot go as far as the Swedish reform, at least if studies are asked for by experts independent of the government the results of such studies will be made available to parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
maintopic: PRINCIPLE OF ACCESSIBILITY OF REPORTS AND STUDIES UNDERTAKEN FOR THE GOVERNMENT BY OUTSIDE PROFESSIONAL GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologise for the tardiness. I understood that I was to answer a question by the second speaker on the list. Unfortunately, I only had the benefit of rereading the initial question asked by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) and I assume he has reiterated his position.
Generally speaking, reports asked for by the government are commissioned on one of two main bases: Either with a view to publication-that is being made public-or with a view to non-nublication. There are a number of instances in which investigations are sought, in which proposals are asked for or information is sought, which it would not be in the public interest to disclose.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Further, there are a number of people, experts of one kind or another from whom advice is sought on a confidential basis and it has been found that these people are prepared to be more frank in expressing their views and opinions when they know that the advice is private rather than to be made public. As a consequence of this, in each case an initial determination is made as to whether the report or the investigation commissioned is for purposes of publication or for the internal use of the government.
On this basis, reports are made public either by mass publication or by tabling in the house in response to a request, if there is one, or through release. An example of the kind of report which was prepared with a view to publication is the recent report of the task force on housing. On the other hand, the report of the commission which inquired into security questions was not prepared with a view to publication as such and consequently it will not be published in its original form.
I think the hon. gentleman will understand that there are basically two categories, and that failure to publish is not motivated by a desire to withhold information from the public domain, but by a wish to secure the best possible range of opinions and views from the person or persons commissioned to carry out the survey or inquiry and to make recommendations.

maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-FEASABILITY STUDY OF GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME
VETERANS AFFAIRS-FEASABILITY STUDY OF GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME
speechtext:
First, I
should like to thank the minister for his courtesy in appearing tonight to reply to the question I raised the other day concerning the feasibility of a guaranteed annual income for veterans. I raised this question particularly since the committee on Veterans Affairs is to examine the Woods report, at which time it will deal with benefits to veterans and the situation facing them at this time.
The idea of a guaranteed annual income is one which is increasingly advocated nowadays. Strangely enough it seems to be supported by both right wing and left wing elements in our society. It is supported by the right wing because its administrative ease is attractive and because of a desire to co-ordinate welfare programs which have become an administrative hodge-podge. We on the left regard it as a simple, elementary form of justice for those who are unable to take care of themselves for whatever reason, or who
[Mr. Drury.)

have been left behind in the competitive rat race of our society.
Thus, both from an administrative point of view and from a humanitarian point of view the idea of a guaranteed annual income is one which in my opinion will become a feature of every western society. I hope we can introduce it for our veterans and in particular for veterans of the first world war. The tragedy of the situation might be this-that the idea of a guaranteed income will be accepted, but accepted too late to be of assistance to veterans of the first world war, and, perhaps, of the second world war also. I suggest its application to veterans at this point not because I believe veterans should, in this context, be singled out for special treatment, but because if a guaranteed annual income is brought in it is likely to be brought in by stages. The first stage would be either an income for everyone at a very low level, or an income at a higher level for specific groups. In looking over the statistics and information relating to veterans in this country, it seems to me we could probably implement such a program without its being too heavy a cost at the moment, giving us the chance to make a start on a guaranteed annual income for everybody.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In the evidence given before the committee it was pointed out that at least 25 to 30 per cent of all veterans in the first world war are now receiving one kind of assistance or another from the department. That figure is quite close to half our first world war veterans. Since we are already bearing the cost in large measure, it seems to me it would be far preferable to extend the guaranteed annual income if only to ensure that some veterans who cannot qualify now would qualify under such program.
Our present legislation is helpful. I think we in Canada can be reasonably pleased at having legislation that is much better than legislation of some other countries in terms of looking after our veterans. But this is not to say that the legislation cannot be improved or that there are not veterans who are suffering unduly at this time.
Recently all members of the house have been receiving letters from Dieppe veterans. The situation was put rather well in a letter I received from one of my constituents. He said:
After being liberated we were so elated with the thought of freedom that upon being discharged we did not submit all of our physical complaints
February 17, 1969	COMMONS
as we thought this would delay matters. I hope you can visualize the situation. Now that we are older, these seemingly trivial aches and pains have turned into serious complaints-a direct result, we believe, of our incarceration. When we seek medical attention we are told, "Sorry there is nothing showing on your record".
That is one of the great defects, if not the major defect, of the present legislation. Either because some veterans were not aware of disabilities they might have had or because they were anxious to leave the service for one reason or another, they were not able to establish a claim. Later on when their problems developed it became very difficult for the department to ascertain whether these problems were attributable to war service. I imagine it is a very difficult situation for the people who administer the act.
I feel quite sympathetic to the Dieppe veterans. I have always felt that in some ways they got a terribly raw deal. I was never convinced that the raid was essential, and I sometimes wonder to what extent it was a deliberate sacrifice on the part of the military in order to quieten the cry for a second front. However, I am pleased that the minister is in the house, and I hope he has had a chance to examine the question I posed to him and that he will provide an answer to the question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Eudes Dube (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-FEASABILITY STUDY OF GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) for his remarks on behalf of the veterans of Canada, especially his comments about the feasibility of a guaranteed income for veterans. As he knows, the Woods report which will be referred to the House of Commons committee on veterans affairs deals with disability pensions and with the Canadian Pension Commission. These matters will, of course, be
DEBATES	5633
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion coming up for study at that time, and I do not wish to anticipate the debate.
Perhaps the hon. member knows, if he does not, then this is an occasion for me to underline the fact, that many if not most of our veterans at the present time do enjoy a guaranteed annual income. Provision for that guarantee is made in the War Veterans Allowance Act which has been in existence since 1930. Of course, I should point out that that act does not apply to most veterans, but only to those who are in dire need. Fortunately, the great majority of the veterans in this country are in no need of having their income supplemented. They are doing very well on their own in our economy. Perhaps the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) will be interested to know that a quarter of all family heads in Canada earning between $4,000 and $5,000, the average income, are veterans. In fact, more than a quarter are veterans. The hon. member may be surprised to learn that in the higher income levels the percentage of veterans earning those incomes increases. Of those earning $10,000 a year, more than 50 per cent are veterans. So, it is with pride that we underline the fact that most of our veterans have adjusted to our society very well and are doing very well on their own.
However, in the case of veterans who cannot find employment in the market perhaps because of disability for which they are receiving pension, the War Veterans Allowance Act will apply. They may receive slightly over $4,000 in income.
